title: Temperature Safety
story: In 1999, NASA's Mars Climate Orbiter burned up because one team used metric and another used imperial. A simple invariant — temperature can't drop below absolute zero — would have flagged the impossible value long before it hit production.
why: Type invariants prevent physically impossible values from ever existing in your program.
analogy: An invariant is like a bouncer at a nightclub door — once you're inside, everyone knows you belong.
try_it: Add a `Temperature.from_fahrenheit` constructor that accepts Fahrenheit and converts back to Celsius, with a `requires` clause that prevents values below -459.67°F (absolute zero in Fahrenheit).
tips: Invariants encode domain physics — if the real world says 'this can't be negative', your type should too
Use `requires` on setters when callers can control the input; let the invariant guard all mutations
Chain conversion methods: to_fahrenheit, to_kelvin, to_rankine — the invariant protects every result
common_mistakes: Writing a setter without `requires` — if the setter takes arbitrary values, the invariant will catch it at mutation time, but a `requires` gives a clearer error earlier
Forgetting that invariants are NOT checked on read-only access — `&self` methods skip invariant checks
